stories.headline: Trump Threatens to Ban Bombardier Jet Sales in U.S. as Canada Trade War Escalates
stories.summary:
President Trump warned Monday that Canadian aircraft manufacturer Bombardier will no longer be permitted to sell planes in the United States unless it relocates manufacturing there. Trump posted the threat on Truth Social, writing "NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!" and accusing Canada of treating America like a "piggybank." The move comes hours before Canada's retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion worth of U.S. goods are set to take effect.

Bombardier pushed back in a statement, noting it employs approximately 3,500 American workers at a Kansas facility and operates sites across ten U.S. states, with roughly half of its global fleet — some 5,100 aircraft — operated by U.S.-based customers. The company said its operations "create tens of thousands of US jobs" and that it values its partnerships with American companies. It did not address Trump's threat directly.

It remains legally unclear how Trump would block Bombardier from doing business in the U.S., given the company's deep American footprint and its aircraft's compliance with the USMCA trade agreement Trump himself signed in his first term. Quebec Premier Christine Frécheette called Bombardier "a source of pride" and said her government would offer full support to the company, adding: "Quebec will not allow anyone to dictate where our companies must produce in order to access a market."

The confrontation marks a sharp escalation in the U.S.-Canada trade war, which collapsed in late August after Canada walked away from negotiations, with Prime Minister Carney citing "unfair" last-minute U.S. demands. U.S. officials countered that Carney refused a deal for domestic political reasons. The standoff now threatens one of Canada's largest companies and a major Quebec employer at a moment when both nations have already imposed sweeping tariffs on each other.

stories.headline: Eiffel Tower Shut After Female Workers Removed for Hindu Religious Group's Visit
stories.summary:
The Eiffel Tower was closed Monday after staff went on strike following the removal of female employees from their posts to accommodate a visiting Hindu religious delegation. A group of approximately 100 people affiliated with the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) visited the landmark on Saturday, during which women were asked to vacate their workplaces so men could be positioned in their places.

The Eiffel Tower's operating company, SETE, confirmed the delegation had requested the visit be organized to limit "interactions with women," but said those conditions "should not have been accepted" and were "not in line with SETE's values, nor with the principles of equality between men and women." SETE president Ariel Weil called the practice "clearly not acceptable" and reaffirmed the monument's commitment to gender equality. Management also apologized to the affected workers.

Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire announced an investigation and said female workers' discontent was "legitimate," declaring that gender equality "must be applied everywhere, for everyone." Far-right leader Marine Le Pen and former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal also condemned the incident. BAPS, in a statement, apologized for "any pain or inconvenience caused" and said its trip was arranged to avoid disrupting normal operations.

The incident has ignited a broader debate in France about the accommodation of religious practices in public institutions and the primacy of secular republican values. The strike forced the closure of one of the world's most visited tourist sites on a Monday in early September, affecting thousands of visitors and drawing condemnation across France's political spectrum.

stories.headline: 9/11 Anniversary Tensions: Giuliani Urges Muslim Mayor Mamdani to Skip Ground Zero Ceremony
stories.summary:
Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani publicly called on current Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who is Muslim, to skip this Friday's 9/11 commemoration at Ground Zero, saying the mayor's attendance would "offend him" and asserting that Mamdani does not accept the attacks as an Islamic terrorist act. Giuliani, who led New York during the September 11, 2001 attacks and became the public face of the city's response, made the remarks in an interview with Newsmax.

Mamdani confirmed he will attend the memorial service marking the 25th anniversary of the attacks but declined to respond directly to Giuliani's remarks. The confrontation sets up a charged face-to-face moment at one of the nation's most solemn annual commemorations. Mamdani, a democratic socialist, became New York City's first Muslim mayor after winning this year's mayoral race.

The episode has drawn sharp reactions across the political spectrum. Critics of Giuliani argue his comments amount to religious discrimination and an attempt to exclude an elected official from a civic ceremony on the basis of his faith. Supporters of Giuliani's position contend the remarks reflect legitimate concerns about ideological consistency at a memorial for victims of Islamist terrorism.

The friction highlights broader tensions around identity, religion, and political leadership in New York City as the country prepares to mark 25 years since the deadliest terrorist attack on U.S. soil. The 9/11 ceremony at Ground Zero draws national attention each year, and Mamdani's presence as the city's Muslim mayor will itself be a historically notable moment.

stories.headline: Update: Canadian Retaliatory Tariffs Set to Take Effect Tuesday as No New Negotiations Reported
stories.summary:
Canada's retaliatory tariffs — matching U.S. levies dollar for dollar — are set to take effect overnight Monday into Tuesday, two weeks after President Trump imposed 50 percent tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian goods. There are no reports of renewed negotiations between Washington and Ottawa, and trade talks that broke down last month have not resumed.

The escalation marks a significant new phase in the U.S.-Canada trade war. Trump has additionally threatened to bar the sale of Bombardier aircraft in the United States, accusing Canada of unfair trade practices. CBS News business analysts warned the new tariffs will have measurable effects on American consumer finances.

Supporters of the Trump administration's tariff strategy argue the measures are necessary to address what they describe as a chronic trade imbalance and unfair Canadian practices. Critics, including some Republicans, have warned the escalating trade fight risks worsening inflation ahead of the midterm elections, with at least one GOP senator saying Congress should address rising prices but that action is 'not likely.'

The Canada-U.S. trade standoff is being watched closely by markets and trading partners globally, as tit-for-tat measures between the two longtime allies represent one of the most serious disruptions to North American trade in decades.

stories.headline: Update: First LNG Tanker Attempts Hormuz Transit Since July as Iran Tightens Chokehold
stories.summary:
A Qatari liquefied natural gas tanker that loaded cargo in late July is making what appears to be the first visible attempt to transit the Strait of Hormuz since the waterway was effectively shut down amid U.S.-Iran hostilities. The move is being closely monitored as a test of whether commercial shipping can resume through the critical chokepoint.

Iran has threatened to impose an 'exclusion zone' outside the strait as part of efforts to restrict tanker traffic, and oil prices have spiked to six-week highs on disruption fears. U.S. military escorts have been operating in the region, and the passage of the Qatari vessel could signal either a partial restoration of flow or provoke a new Iranian response.

The Strait of Hormuz handles a significant share of the world's oil and LNG exports, making its status a matter of acute global economic concern. Earlier reporting indicated strait oil flows were nearing pre-war levels under military escort, but Iran's threatened exclusion zone introduces new uncertainty into that picture.

Separately, Ukraine reported overnight strikes on oil-processing facilities in Russia's Perm region and Tatarstan, resuming attacks after U.S. envoys completed visits to both Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.

stories.headline: New Hampshire Democrats at Risk of Losing Senate Seat as Sununu Gains Ahead of Tuesday Primary
stories.summary:
New Hampshire voters head to the polls Tuesday in a primary that could determine the balance of power in the U.S. Senate. The state has not elected a Republican senator in 16 years, but Democrats are now considered at risk of losing the seat to Chris Sununu, the scion of a prominent New Hampshire political dynasty.

The race has drawn national attention because Democratic control of the Senate could hinge on the outcome. Sununu, who previously served as governor, has built a broad political profile and is seen as a strong general-election candidate in a state that has trended competitive in recent cycles.

The New Hampshire contest is part of a broader midterm environment described as volatile, with Democrats holding a significant party-affiliation advantage nationally but facing headwinds in specific competitive states. Republicans have targeted the seat as a top pickup opportunity.

The outcome of Tuesday's primary will clarify the field heading into the November general election, which analysts view as one of the most consequential Senate races of the midterm cycle.

stories.headline: Serbia Heads to Snap Election as Vucic Seeks to Consolidate Power After Months of Protests
stories.summary:
Serbian Prime Minister Milos Vucevic has called for the dissolution of parliament, paving the way for a snap election widely seen as an attempt by embattled President Aleksandar Vucic to strengthen his grip on power. The move follows months of large-scale street protests against Vucic's government.

Analysts view the election as a bid by Vucic to potentially switch from the presidency to the role of prime minister, a constitutional maneuver that could allow him to exercise more direct control over the government while resetting his political mandate. Opposition groups have accused Vucic of using the snap vote to suppress the momentum of the protest movement.

The protests that preceded the election call were among the largest in Serbia in years, driven by public anger over governance failures, corruption allegations, and a deadly infrastructure collapse. The opposition has struggled to translate street energy into unified electoral force against Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party.

Serbia's political trajectory has implications for the broader Balkans region and for European Union accession negotiations, which have stalled under Vucic's leadership even as Belgrade has maintained ambiguous ties with Moscow.

stories.headline: Update: Russia-Ukraine Peace Talks End With Symbolism but No Breakthrough as Fundamental Gaps Persist
stories.summary:
U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at Kyiv's Saint Sophia Cathedral on Monday, marking the first time Trump's diplomatic team has set foot on Ukrainian soil since Russia's full-scale invasion began. The envoys arrived by train, unable to fly due to the risk from Russian drones — the same weapons Moscow had used to strike Ukraine's security service headquarters nearby just days earlier. All parties described the discussions as substantive, and talks were later joined by European national security advisers including the UK's Jonathan Powell.

Despite the historic symbolism, fundamental disagreements remain unresolved. Coming directly from Moscow, where Vladimir Putin told them Russia was making battlefield advances and insisted on addressing the conflict's "root causes" — diplomatic shorthand for demands that Ukraine cede territory, abandon NATO aspirations, and reduce its military — the envoys received a starkly different account in Kyiv. Ukrainian officials claim they gained more territory than they lost in August and that Russia suffered 42,000 casualties in the same period.

Zelensky insisted Ukraine requires "strong and clear" security guarantees and gave no indication of willingness to surrender territory in the Donbas. Witkoff acknowledged both sides would need to make compromises but expressed optimism that the ingredients for a settlement exist. A short-term pause in air strikes tied to the talks has provided Kyiv brief relief, though few expect it to hold.

Diplomats in Kyiv broadly expect fighting to continue through the winter, with some holding out hope for a possible settlement window next spring. Others are less optimistic. The talks represent a new development on a previously covered story: this is the first confirmed face-to-face meeting between Trump envoys and Zelensky on Ukrainian soil, adding a concrete diplomatic milestone even as the substantive impasse continues.

stories.headline: Russia Orders German Consulate in St. Petersburg Closed in Tit-for-Tat Escalation Over Leipzig Drone Attack
stories.summary:
Russia's Foreign Ministry announced Monday that Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg must cease operations and its staff must leave Russia by September 18, the latest escalation in a bilateral dispute rooted in an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4. Germany had already closed the Russian consulate in Bonn and the Russian House cultural center in Berlin last week, citing Moscow's responsibility for the airport incident, in which an explosives-laden drone was found near a Ukrainian aircraft and later defused.

Russia also reaffirmed its earlier decision to shut down German Goethe-Institut cultural centers in both Moscow and St. Petersburg, ordering their employees to depart by Sunday. Moscow denied involvement in the Leipzig attack, calling Germany's response a provocation and placing full responsibility for the diplomatic deterioration on Berlin. The German airport is a major international freight hub used to support Ukraine.

The exchange marks a significant new rupture in German-Russian relations and fits a broader pattern Western governments have identified: a sustained Russian campaign of sabotage and disruption across European nations aimed at undermining support for Ukraine. Moscow has consistently denied those allegations.

The closure of a formal consulate — not merely a cultural center — raises the diplomatic stakes considerably and signals that the conflict in Ukraine continues to fracture Russia's relationships with major European powers beyond the battlefield.

stories.headline: Trump Promises Midterm Victory, Attacks Democrats in Labor Day Message as RNC Convention Approaches
stories.summary:
President Trump used Labor Day on Monday to issue a combative social media message targeting Democrats, promising Republican victory in the upcoming midterm elections and describing opponents as "Radical Left Lunatics, Communists, and Dumocrats" seeking to destroy the country. The message came as Trump is confirmed to appear on both nights of the Republican National Committee's inaugural midterm convention in Dallas — delivering the first night's keynote address and closing remarks on the second night.

The RNC's decision to hold a midterm convention is itself a novel political move, drawing historical comparisons to Jimmy Carter's 1978 Democratic midterm gathering in Memphis, which became a launching pad for Ted Kennedy's insurgent challenge. Republicans are framing the Dallas event as a show of party unity behind Trump heading into what are expected to be highly competitive congressional races.

Democrats and independent analysts have noted that Trump enters the midterms with historically low approval ratings, and recent Gallup data showed Democrats holding their largest party-affiliation advantage since 2008. The GOP is countering that narrative with high-profile Senate investments, including a $10 million super-PAC push in Texas, where Ken Paxton's nomination has drawn intraparty skepticism.

The Labor Day messaging underscores the degree to which Trump himself remains the central figure in Republican midterm strategy — a double-edged dynamic that energizes the base but presents challenges in swing districts where independent voters have shown wariness toward his style.

stories.headline: Prediction Markets Face Supreme Court as New Jersey Urges Justices to Settle Regulatory Dispute
stories.summary:
New Jersey this past week formally urged the U.S. Supreme Court to resolve how prediction markets — platforms where users bet real money on the outcomes of political, economic, and other events — should be regulated, setting up a potential landmark ruling on an industry that has grown rapidly in recent years. A circuit split among federal appeals courts is raising expectations that the justices will take up the case, with the Trump administration seeking to keep prediction markets under federal oversight and push states out of the regulatory picture.

The dispute centers on whether platforms such as Kalshi constitute regulated futures exchanges under federal commodities law or fall under state gambling statutes. The Trump administration has sided with federal jurisdiction, while states including New Jersey argue they retain authority to regulate or restrict such platforms. The outcome will determine the legal status of an industry that attracted significant attention during the 2024 and 2026 election cycles as an alternative gauge of public sentiment.

The case carries broader implications for both the gambling industry and financial markets, as prediction markets increasingly blur the line between speculative trading and regulated wagering. High-profile controversies — including former Congressman George Santos being banned from Kalshi after accusations of manipulating markets — have added political visibility to the legal fight.

With three outlets tracking the story and a formal petition now before the Court, the regulatory future of prediction markets may hinge on whether the justices agree to hear what would be a closely watched and commercially consequential case.

stories.headline: Update: Kyiv Endures Record Air Raid Alerts as Russia Deploys Faster Jet-Powered Drones
stories.summary:
Kyiv is experiencing more daily air raid alerts than at any point since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, according to BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian government data. In the seven days ending September 3, the capital logged 76 air raid alerts, surpassing the previous record of roughly 66 set in the first days of the invasion. Residents are being forced into shelters as many as 13 times a day, disrupting schools, businesses, and public transit.

A key driver of the escalation is Russia's increasing use of jet-powered attack drones flying at up to 370 mph — roughly three times the speed of older propeller-driven Shahed drones — making them significantly harder to intercept. Russia launched approximately 2,800 of the faster drones in August, nearly double the July total. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky held an emergency meeting with ministers and military commanders to accelerate development of high-speed interceptor missiles capable of countering the new threat.

Military analysts warn that Russia may be able to manufacture the fast drones more quickly than Ukraine can develop countermeasures, potentially making this threat more dangerous than Russian ballistic missiles. Ukraine is currently relying on warplanes, anti-aircraft guns, and shoulder-launched missiles to respond. A brief pause in attacks on Kyiv occurred over the weekend while U.S. envoys were in the capital for war-ending talks, but strikes resumed once diplomats departed.

In response to the round-the-clock nature of the attacks, the Ukrainian government is planning a new two-tier alert system that would allow citizens to continue working, studying, and traveling based on the assessed scale of each threat, rather than halting all activity with every siren.

stories.headline: Grindr to Pay £26 Million to Settle Claims It Shared Users' HIV Status and Sensitive Data
stories.summary:
Grindr, the world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app, has agreed to pay £26 million to settle a class-action lawsuit alleging it unlawfully shared users' sensitive personal information — including HIV status, ethnicity, and sexual orientation — with third-party data analytics firms. The settlement, disclosed in a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing dated September 2, involves two payments of £13 million each and includes no admission of liability.

The lawsuit, brought in the UK High Court in 2024 by law firm Austen Hayes, had more than 11,000 claimants. The firm alleged that Grindr shared data with analytics services Apptimize and Localytics for commercial advertising purposes, breaching UK privacy laws. The underlying data-sharing practices were first publicly revealed in 2018, during a period when Grindr was owned by Chinese firm Kunlun; Grindr says the conduct predates its current ownership and that it has since overhauled its privacy practices.

Grindr was previously fined £5.5 million by Norway's data protection authority and reprimanded by the UK's Information Commissioner's Office for the same conduct. The company stated it 'recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users' but maintained the settlement does not constitute an admission of wrongdoing.

The case highlights ongoing legal and regulatory risks for tech companies that monetize sensitive personal data, particularly in jurisdictions with strict privacy frameworks. Claimants' lawyers said Grindr 'owes it to the LGBTQ+ community it serves to compensate those whose data has been compromised.'

stories.headline: FIFA's Infantino Confirms Re-Election Bid Despite UEFA Criminal Complaint Threat
stories.summary:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino has confirmed he will stand for re-election in 2027, seeking a final term through 2031, despite significant institutional pressure to resign following the collapse of his controversial plan to sell stakes in future World Cup revenues to private investors. FIFA issued a statement Sunday confirming Infantino's candidacy, citing an April announcement of his intentions.

The backlash against Infantino has been led by UEFA, European soccer's governing body, which said it lost confidence in the FIFA president and threatened to boycott FIFA tournaments including the World Cup. UEFA is now preparing a criminal complaint against Infantino in Swiss courts over possible financial mismanagement related to the abandoned commercial plan. Several prominent national football associations, including England's FA, have also withdrawn their support for his re-election.

FIFA apologized for procedural errors in how the World Cup equity plan was handled and pledged reforms, but that response has not satisfied critics. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham publicly stated last month that Infantino was not the right leader for world soccer. The November 18 deadline for candidates to enter the presidential race gives potential challengers roughly ten weeks to mount opposition campaigns.

Infantino's continued candidacy sets up a potentially historic confrontation between FIFA and UEFA, the most powerful regional confederation in world soccer, ahead of the 2026 World Cup hosted jointly by the United States, Canada, and Mexico.

stories.headline: Update: Iran War Has Cost U.S. Consumers $100 Billion in Higher Energy Prices
stories.summary:
The ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict has driven energy costs up by $100 billion for American consumers, according to a real-time tracker from Brown University's Watson Institute, with costs rising at roughly $1 million every two minutes as of Monday. The national average for regular gasoline hit $4.15 per gallon over Labor Day weekend — a record high for that holiday — while diesel prices reached an all-time record of $5.90 per gallon. The average U.S. household has spent an estimated $763 more on fuel over the six-month conflict.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright appeared on Sunday political shows cautiously predicting gasoline price relief ahead, but declined to offer firm timelines or specific figures. Wright also told ABC News that a nuclear agreement with Iran may not materialize despite months of conflict. Meanwhile, Iran announced plans to declare a restricted zone near the Strait of Hormuz, potentially tightening its chokehold on tanker traffic, though details remain sparse.

The economic ripple effects are significant beyond the pump: elevated diesel prices threaten to raise freight and travel costs across the broader economy in the weeks ahead, with the midterm elections now less than two months away. Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana acknowledged his party needs to address inflation but said action is 'not likely.' An NBC News poll found that the share of Republicans who strongly approve of Trump's management of the Iran war has dropped significantly in recent months.

Supporters of the administration argue the conflict was necessary to counter Iranian aggression and that market forces will eventually bring prices down as the military situation stabilizes. Critics contend the war's economic toll on working Americans is unsustainable and that the administration lacks a clear exit strategy, with Energy Secretary Wright himself acknowledging uncertainty over a diplomatic resolution.

stories.headline: Leaked Texts Show Sen. Fetterman Dismissing Constituent Service, Skipping Funerals and Hospital Meetings
stories.summary:
Text messages obtained by The Wall Street Journal and confirmed by CBS News reveal that Pennsylvania Democratic Sen. John Fetterman has repeatedly refused or dismissed core senatorial duties, including meeting with constituents, holding events in Pennsylvania, and attending congressional hearings. In one exchange, Fetterman told a staffer he would not meet with Children's Hospital of Philadelphia representatives, writing 'I'm convinced they just want free trips to DC.' In another, he described attending the funerals of three slain police officers near his hometown as a potential 'nonstarter' due to the length of the ceremony and travel time.

A former staffer confirmed the accuracy of the Journal's reporting to CBS News and said substantive policy conversations with Fetterman consistently became 'completely derailed or unhinged.' The revelation adds to existing scrutiny of Fetterman, who suffered a serious stroke during his 2022 Senate campaign and has faced intermittent questions about his capacity to serve.

Fetterman responded to CNN over the weekend, saying the texts were 'stripped of any context and circumstances.' He called his remarks about the children's hospital a 'dumb joke' and apologized for them, while stating he has met with hospital officials both virtually and in person. Regarding the police funerals, he said his office sent flowers to the families and that he later attended a private fundraiser in York to honor the officers.

The story carries political weight in Pennsylvania, a key battleground state, as Fetterman has increasingly positioned himself as a centrist Democrat willing to break with his party on immigration and other issues. His Senate seat will be on the ballot in 2028, and the revelations could complicate his standing with both progressive and moderate voters.

stories.headline: Thousands Attend State Funeral of Convicted War Criminal Ratko Mladic in Serbia, EU Warns Against Glorification
stories.summary:
Thousands of people gathered in Belgrade on Monday for the funeral of Ratko Mladic, the Bosnian Serb military commander convicted of genocide and war crimes by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. The event was held with what observers described as state honors, drawing an outpouring of nationalist sentiment in Serbia despite international condemnation.

The European Union issued a warning against glorifying Mladic, who was convicted in 2017 for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre — in which more than 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were killed — as well as for the siege of Sarajevo and other atrocities during the 1990s Balkan wars. The EU warning reflects ongoing tension between Serbia's EU membership aspirations and the country's relationship with figures from its wartime past.

The funeral underscores the persistent divide between Serbia and its neighbors, particularly Bosnia and Herzegovina, where survivors and victims' families reacted with outrage to the public honors accorded to Mladic. Bosnia's government has not yet issued a formal statement as of Monday morning.

The event has broader implications for European stability and the Western Balkans' fragile post-war reconciliation process. Serbia is an EU candidate country, and the bloc has repeatedly pressed Belgrade to confront its wartime legacy as a condition of closer integration.

stories.headline: New Videos Emerge in 9/11 Lawsuit Showing Key Figure's Ties to Saudi Officials and Al-Qaeda Leader
stories.summary:
Previously unseen videos obtained by BBC Panorama show Omar al-Bayoumi — a central figure in a $1 trillion lawsuit brought by 9/11 families against Saudi Arabia — embracing Anwar al-Awlaki, who later led al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, and paintballing near San Diego with a Saudi Ministry of Islamic Affairs official. The footage, which the FBI obtained within days of the September 11, 2001 attacks, directly contradicts Bayoumi's 25-year denial that he had extremist links or served as a Saudi intelligence asset.

Also discovered among Bayoumi's possessions at the time of his arrest in the United Kingdom was a diagram of a plane with a flight descent equation — evidence that was never shared with British interrogators or the 9/11 Commission, according to BBC reporting. FBI agents in San Diego repeatedly requested copies of key evidence but were denied access, and they were also blocked from interviewing Bayoumi's Saudi government contacts.

The lawsuit, which a judge allowed to proceed in 2018, argues that Saudi Arabia was complicit in the attacks and that Bayoumi aided two of the 19 hijackers. Thousands of documents have since been declassified through an executive order by former President Biden. A former U.S. Department of Justice official told the BBC that despite the evidence, he was never presented with a prosecution proposal for Bayoumi, adding 'we've convicted people for less.'

Bayoumi was never prosecuted and was released after his arrest in Britain. He and the Saudi government have consistently denied any involvement in or foreknowledge of the attacks. The FBI declined to comment on the BBC's findings. With the 25th anniversary of the attacks approaching, the new footage is likely to intensify pressure on both the U.S. government and Saudi Arabia to provide fuller accounting of the events leading up to September 11.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Warns of 'Faster, Heavier' Response as U.S.-Iran Conflict Intensifies
stories.summary:
Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned Sunday of "a faster, heavier, and more painful response" to U.S. strikes, saying Americans must understand "before it is too late" that the "rules of the game have changed." The warning came as Iranian state media claimed the country's Navy attacked an American remote-controlled vessel attempting to enter the Strait of Hormuz — a claim the U.S. military flatly denied. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reiterated that any Iranian attack on U.S. ships would result in the destruction of Iranian oil tankers.

The new development marks a material escalation in rhetoric following a week of renewed fighting after a 60-day ceasefire expired last month. The U.S. has launched multiple strikes on Iranian oil tankers, and Iran has retaliated against American targets in the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Jordan. The Strait of Hormuz, effectively closed since the conflict began in February, remains a central flashpoint.

The economic toll is mounting for American consumers: the average price of diesel in the U.S. hit $5.85 per gallon Friday, up from $3.71 a year ago. U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday that roughly 9 million barrels of oil per day are now moving through the strait, representing about two-thirds of pre-conflict flows, which he said could help ease energy prices.

President Trump said this week the renewed fighting would not last "too long," but months of negotiations have yielded no lasting peace agreement, and diplomatic officials see little prospect of an imminent settlement.

stories.headline: Update: Israeli Strikes in Southern Lebanon Kill Nine, Including Child, as Ceasefire Frays
stories.summary:
Israeli airstrikes on the southern Lebanese village of Kfar Remman killed at least nine people overnight, including a child, a woman, and a paramedic, according to Lebanon's health ministry. One strike destroyed a three-story residential building, killing eight; a second hit a vehicle carrying paramedics, killing one. Eleven others were wounded. The Israeli military said it was looking into the reports; the Israeli foreign ministry accused Hezbollah of "repeated drone attacks" and attempting to rebuild its military capabilities in violation of the ceasefire agreement.

The strikes are part of an intensified Israeli military campaign in southern Lebanon over recent days, targeting areas near the strip of territory occupied by Israeli troops. Large numbers of residents have again been fleeing the region. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun condemned the attacks as a "dangerous escalation" jeopardizing the U.S.-brokered ceasefire reached in June and urged international pressure on Israel to stop.

The ceasefire framework calls for Hezbollah to disarm, Israeli forces to gradually withdraw from southern Lebanon, and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area. Lebanon was drawn into the broader regional conflict on March 2 when Hezbollah — backed by Iran — entered the fighting. The health ministry said the death toll represented "irrefutable evidence of grave violations of international law."

The strikes come amid broader regional instability tied to the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict. Sunday's strikes in Kfar Remman followed attacks the previous day that killed seven people across southern Lebanon.

stories.headline: Update: Anak Krakatau Eruption Strands 270,000 Passengers as Indonesian Airport Closures Extend Into Second Day
stories.summary:
The eruption of Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano has left approximately 270,000 passengers stranded after canceling more than 2,000 flights and forcing airport closures into a second day. Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and three other facilities extended shutdowns until 18:00 local time Monday after volcanic ash was detected in nearby airspaces. Schools in the region moved to online classes and some shipping operations were disrupted.

The volcano, located roughly 150 kilometers from Jakarta in the Sunda Strait, began erupting late Friday, producing lava fountains and sending ash as high as 15,000 meters on the Sumatra side. Indonesia's Geological Agency warned Monday that "the probability of further eruptions in the coming periods remains high." The eruption has affected travelers across the archipelago, with stranded passengers facing days-long delays and scrambling for alternative transport.

The scale of disruption has grown substantially since the story was first reported, with the stranded passenger count rising from 150,000 to 270,000 and closures expanding. A newly wed Malaysian couple in Bali was told the next available flight home to Kuala Lumpur would not depart until September 11.

stories.headline: China Injects $54 Billion Into State Banks and Insurers to Shore Up Slowing Economy
stories.summary:
China's finance ministry announced Sunday it will inject 360 billion yuan ($53.6 billion) into eight state-owned banks and insurance companies, including the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China and the Agricultural Bank of China. State news agency Xinhua said the move is designed to enhance the institutions' "sound operating capabilities, risk resistance capabilities, and ability to serve the real economy." The package marks Beijing's latest effort to reinvigorate the world's second-largest economy.

China faces a confluence of headwinds: a years-long property market slump, a shrinking workforce, trade tensions with the West, and the economic impact of the ongoing U.S.-Iran war on global oil prices. GDP growth slowed to 4.3 percent in the second quarter, below Beijing's already-reduced annual target range of 4.5 to 5 percent — the lowest growth goal set by the government since 1991.

State media outlet Global Times said the capital injection would give financial institutions more resources to channel into credit for the broader economy "while strengthening their ability to withstand external shocks at a time of global financial uncertainty." President Xi Jinping has repeatedly identified financial stability as central to China's national security.
